site: Tikal, Petén, Guatemala. Temple I (Structure 5D-1, the Temple of the Great Jaguar, also called the Temple of Ah Cacao), the funerary pyramid of Jasaw Chan K'awiil I (reigned 682-734). It stands on the east side of the Great Plaza and faces west across it to Temple II. Building it on the east side broke with the older custom of raising royal funerary temples in the North Acropolis, just north of the plaza (Wikipedia, 'Tikal Temple I', lead). Chapter 6, The Americas.
view: Stand on the Great Plaza lawn, a little west of its centre, at a standing person's eye height, and look due east at the west face of Temple I. Show it face-on, or turned very slightly so that the right-hand (south) flanks catch the sun. The pyramid's base sits across the lower middle of the plate, on the lawn. Temple I fills about four fifths of the plate height, so the summit shrine and roof comb stand against the sky with room above the comb. Rainforest canopy fills the plate behind the pyramid and on both sides of it, and its top edge stays well below the summit shrine. Keep the plaza lawn open across the bottom, with nothing between the viewer and the stair. Cropped out: Temple II (it is behind the viewer, across the plaza), the North Acropolis (to the left) and the Central Acropolis (to the right). Why this view: it is the only one that shows all of the vignette's facts in one outline (the nine terraces, the single central stair, the one door and the comb). Nothing modern stands in frame: no visitor, no sign, and no contemporary Maya ceremonial altar or fire circle (see gate6). A brochure is drawn to the face-on elevation. The famous canopy view from Temple IV turns Temple I into a small comb poking out of the trees, which becomes a smudge at 92 x 70. A view from the North Acropolis that fits both temples in gives two stepped masses side-on, the same trap Abu Simbel's baboon frieze was left off to avoid.

elements.fact: Nine stepped terraces, each set back from the one below. Steep: a tall, narrow stepped mass, not a broad low one (whether the whole monument is strictly taller than its base is wide is not measured in anything reached; see contested). Limestone. Sources: 'nine vertiginously steep tiers' and 'a nine-tiered pyramidal structure' (search-result text attributed to Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple I' and a Tikal site description), 'nine tiers' (secondary teaching text), 'nine stepped levels' (travel text), '9 tiers, or terraces' (travel blog); limestone (Wikipedia, 'Tikal' and 'Tikal Temple I').

One stair only, on the front (west) face. It is centred and straight, running from the plaza floor to the summit shrine. The sides and back have no stair. It faces the Great Plaza and Temple II. State today: only a short reconstructed run of steps survives at the foot of the central stair, 'which shows what the original stairway used to look like' (travel account, search snippet); above that the stair is not a clean flight but a rough, unrestored band up the middle of the terraces. Climbing it is restricted.

A single masonry building on top of the ninth terrace. It has three chambers, each behind the next, reached through a single doorway, with the doorways spanned by wooden lintels of several beams. The outer lintel is plain; the two inner ones were carved (Kelly 1996, p.133, via Wikipedia). From outside only ONE doorway shows: a dark opening centred above the stair. The shrine can be no wider than the terrace it stands on.

Masonry, not wood. It rises from the shrine's roof and is no wider than the shrine. Built as two framework walls leaning on one another with an enclosed, vaulted hollow between them to save weight, faced with carved stone and covered with stucco (Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple I' and Uncovered History, via search snippets). Its front carried a monumental seated figure of the king flanked by scrolls and serpents; 'little of this decoration survives' (Miller 1999, p.27, via Wikipedia) and the figure 'now is difficult to discern' (search snippet). Paint it as a closed, weathered, tall block with rough projecting stubs and no readable figure. It holds up nothing.

Bare weathered limestone, weathered dark in streaks and patches, with lighter consolidated areas. No surviving plaster coat or paint shows at this scale. The exterior was stuccoed and some of it painted: red paint is reported on the stucco of the roof comb and on Lintel 3 (search summary of Penn Museum Expedition texts, pages not opened), but no source reached gives a colour scheme for the whole building, so do not paint it red. The grey tone of the bare stone today rests on standard photographs, not re-opened this session.

An open plaza at the foot of the stair, a lawn today. The plaza is flanked east and west by the two great temple-pyramids, with the North Acropolis to the north and the Central Acropolis to the south (Coe 1999, p.123, via Wikipedia). No trees stand in front of the pyramid. Contemporary Maya ceremonies are held in the plaza (see gate6): none is shown, and no modern altar or fire circle is drawn.

Tikal lies in the tropical rainforest of northern Guatemala: kapok (Ceiba pentandra), tropical cedar and Honduras mahogany are among its trees (Wikipedia, Tikal). The canopy stands behind and beside the temple, and the shrine and comb rise clear above it against the sky.

About 38 m tall, on a base of about 37.6 x 41 m (Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple II', via search snippet). It stands on the west side of the plaza facing Temple I, so from this viewpoint it is behind the viewer and NOT in the frame.
The set's shared brochure sky (B.C.skyTop / skyLow), with a fair-weather cloud or two.

deliberatelyWrong: The stair is a ruled band with a few light horizontal strokes, heavier at its foot where the reconstructed steps are, not a countable run of treads. At 368 x 280 its dozens of steps would be sub-pixel, and a wrong count would be a false claim. The unrestored upper stair is rougher than the band suggests.

Each terrace is a plain setback with a lit top and a shadowed face. The mouldings on the terrace faces and the treatment of their corners are left off at this size. Say so in the note, so that nobody reads plain corners as a claim.

The North Acropolis (left) and the Central Acropolis (right) are left out, and the canopy runs in where they stand. At 92 x 70 a second stepped mass beside Temple I would merge with its outline. This is the same reasoning as the baboon frieze at Abu Simbel.
The brochure sky is cleaner and bluer than any real Petén sky, and the lawn is tidier than the real one (shared set convention).
The canopy is simplified to a band of rounded crowns. No particular tree is claimed.
Temple II is omitted even though it is the plaza's other half. It stands behind the viewer from this spot, so leaving it out is correct for the viewpoint, and the note should say why it is absent.
The shrine and comb are composed to stand clear of the canopy against the sky. That is the brochure's framing from the plaza, not a measured sight line.

lighting: Afternoon sun from the upper right, the house direction (B.LIGHT = 0.6, -0.8), and here it is also the true light. Temple I faces west onto the plaza, so its front is lit only after noon. Between the September and March equinoxes the afternoon sun at Tikal's 17 degrees N stands in the south-west, which is behind the right shoulder of a viewer facing east. Result: the front face is in sun, the right-hand (south) flanks of each terrace and the terrace tops are brightest, and the left-hand (north) flanks are in cool shade (B.shade). The doorway is black. The comb's projecting stubs throw small shadows down and to the left. The pyramid casts its shadow down-left onto the lawn (B.castShadow). A morning view would be backlit, with the whole front in shadow, and no brochure prints that.
pitfalls: Painting Temple II beside Temple I. The two face each other across the plaza, east and west. From the stair's side, Temple II is behind you.
Giving it four stairs like El Castillo at Chichén Itzá. Temple I has one, on the west face only.

A roof comb that is openwork or pierced, like the combs at Palenque. Temple I's comb is two leaning walls with an enclosed vaulted hollow between them (Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple I', via search snippet), so from the front it reads as a closed block. Check the outline against Maler 1911 or Maudslay before painting.
A wooden roof comb. At least one online dataset says 'carved wooden roof comb'. The comb is masonry; only the door lintels were wood.

A seated king, a jaguar or any readable figure on the comb or the façade. The comb's giant seated king, once flanked by scrolls and serpents, is almost entirely lost. The 'Great Jaguar' of the nickname comes from a carved wooden lintel inside the shrine showing the king on a jaguar throne (Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple I', lead). That lintel is not on the outside, and parts of the lintels were taken to European museums in the 19th century.
A shrine wider than the top terrace (the current code does this), or a flat-topped pyramid with no shrine.
A broad, low pyramid. Temple I is steep: nine steep tiers under a tall shrine and comb.
Yellow sandstone like Egypt, white restored plaster, or all-over red. Today it is grey stone.

The 19th-century state. Maudslay's (1881-82) and Maler's photographs show it overgrown with trees growing out of the terraces. Use them for the geometry, not the surface. The brochure shows it cleared, as it has been since the University of Pennsylvania project (1956-1970).
Trees or undergrowth in front of the stair. The plaza is open.
Several doorways on the shrine. There is one; the three rooms lie one behind another.
Adding tourists, the climbing chain or rope of past decades, or signage. Climbing is restricted today, and none of it belongs in a brochure plate.
A crisp, complete flight of steps. Only a short reconstructed run survives at the foot; the rest of the stair is a rough unrestored band.
A modern Maya ceremonial altar, fire circle, candles or offerings in the plaza. Ceremonies are held at Tikal today (see gate6); none belongs in the plate.
gate6: FLAG: needs a designer ruling before this vignette is painted. Temple I itself is a ruin of the Classic Maya religion and the funerary monument of an 8th-century king; Jasaw Chan K'awiil I's tomb (Burial 116) was excavated in 1962, so it is not a grave of the recently dead. But the site is not only a ruin: contemporary Maya spiritual guides hold ceremonies at Tikal, including in the Great Plaza. Confirmed this session from search snippets only (pages blocked): a Maya fire ceremony closing a seven-day, seven-site cycle was held in the central plaza of Tikal on 21 December 2009; a contemporary Maya altar on site is described as where 'various Maya ritual ceremonies are currently celebrated', led by a spiritual guide; ceremonial fires are lit in the Great Plaza at the December solstice (Smithsonian NMAI, Living Maya Time); and Guatemala's Ministry of Culture and Sports issues authorisations for Maya spiritual ceremonies in archaeological parks and sites (Acuerdo Ministerial 981-2011 on spiritual guides, 1171-2012 on visitor conduct). Under arc.md section 1 that makes Tikal an ambiguous case, and arc.md chapter 6 does not yet flag it. It belongs in arc.md section 4 for a ruling, not in a level designer's or painter's hands. Recommendation, on the Borobudur and Great Zimbabwe pattern: architecture, lawn and forest only; no people, no ceremony, no contemporary altar or fire circle, no candles or offerings in frame, on the tour map and in any level. Temple I is the ancient monument, not the ceremonial locus, so the vignette as specified already meets that recommendation.
contested: Height. 47 m (154 ft) in Wikipedia citing Martin & Grube 2000, and in most modern popular sources. 145 ft (44 m) in art-history survey texts; one search snippet prints '145 feet (47 meters)', mixing the two. A search summary also gave '55 m over the Great Plaza', probably conflated with Temple III (55 m in Wikipedia 'Tikal'); disregard it unless a measured source says so. The difference is probably the measuring base and the top point used. Keep 47 m and 44 m in the note and draw no ruler.

Proportion. 'Taller than its base is wide' is not measured in any source reached: Temple I's base dimensions were not found. For comparison, Temple II is about 38 m tall on a 37.6 x 41 m base (Wikipedia, via search snippet); Temple I is some 9 m taller, which suggests but does not prove a height at least equal to its base width. Check against a measured elevation (Tikal Reports, Coe's handbook, or Maler's or Maudslay's plates) before stating it.

Date and builder. Jasaw Chan K'awiil I reigned 682-734 and was entombed in the structure in AD 734 (Martin & Grube 2000, p.43). Wikipedia 'Tikal Temple I' dates the structure to 'approximately 732 AD'; Wikipedia 'Tikal' gives completion 'around 740-750' (Webster 2002), which would put much of it under his son Yik'in Chan K'awiil (reigned 734-766). A Tikal description calls it 'mid eighth century'; art-history captions print 'ca. 700 C.E.'. Write it as 'raised over the tomb of Jasaw Chan K'awiil I, who died in 734; dated c. 732 in some sources and completed c. 740-750 in others'.

Nine terraces as the nine levels of the underworld. This is a popular interpretation ('probably refer to'; '9 is one of the holy numbers of the Maya'), not a documented Maya statement. Keep it out of anything stated as fact.

Temple II and the queen. Older Wikipedia text says Jasaw's wife, Lady Twelve Macaw, is entombed in Temple II. The current text says Temple II was dedicated to her but no tomb was found. This only matters if the note mentions Temple II.

Original colour. Maya buildings were stuccoed and painted; red is reported on the stucco of Temple I's roof comb and on Lintel 3 (search summary of Penn Museum Expedition texts, not opened). No source reached gives the whole building's scheme. Do not assert an all-over red, and do not paint it.
Stone tone today. 'Grey' comes from standard photographs, not re-opened this session. The palette is a neutral grey-buff; check it against a colour photograph before painting.
Stair angle. Travel texts give '70 degrees' for the stair. Unmeasured; do not state it.

repoCorrections: src/map/monuments.ts 'roof-comb': the summit shrine, box(34, 20, 32, 14), is 32 wide, but the ninth terrace it stands on is 74 - 8*5.6 = 29.2 wide (x 35.4 to 64.6). The shrine overhangs the top of the pyramid by 1.4 on each side. Corbelled Maya masonry does not cantilever, and the shrine must be no wider than its terrace.

src/map/monuments.ts 'roof-comb': the proportions are squat. The whole drawing is 70 units tall on a 74-unit base, but Temple I is steep: nine steep tiers under a tall shrine and comb. Whether it is strictly taller than wide is not measured in anything reached (see contested); at least make it no wider than tall.

content/map/README.md, the chapter 6 row, and the monuments.ts comment call the roof comb 'carrying nothing and holding up nothing'. Holding up nothing is right. Carrying nothing is wrong about what it was for: it was built to carry a giant sculpture of the enthroned king, of which little survives (Miller 1999, p.27). Suggest 'holding up nothing, and carrying almost nothing now of the giant seated king it was built for'.

content/map/README.md, chapter 6 row, and the monuments.ts comment: 'a roof comb ... taller than it [the temple]' could not be verified this session. Keep it only after checking a measured elevation (Tikal Reports or Coe's handbook) or Maler's or Maudslay's plates. The claim 'narrower than the temple' is consistent with what I could find.
